note: Hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and cleft palate are canonical craniofacial features across LDS subtypes including SMAD2-associated LDS6, though precise cohort frequencies require deeper investigation.

evidence.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome typically presents with a triad of hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate, and aortic aneurysms with arterial tortuosity, with SMAD2 recognized among the causal TGF-beta pathway genes.

source.title: Loeys-dietz syndrome
source.quote: The most typical clinical triad includes hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate and aortic aneurysm with tortuosity. Natural history is significant for aortic dissection at smaller aortic diameter and arterial aneurysms throughout the arterial tree. The genetic cause is heterogeneous and includes mutations in genes encoding for components of the transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ) signalling pathway: TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFB2 and TGFB3.

evidence.text: SMAD2 is confirmed as an LDS-associated gene, though relatively few mutation-positive cases had been characterized in detail compared to other LDS subtypes.

source.title: A mutation update on the LDS‐associated genes TGFB2/3 and SMAD2/3
source.quote: Most typically, LDS patients present with aortic aneurysms and arterial tortuosity, hypertelorism, and bifid/broad uvula or cleft palate. Initially, mutations in transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) receptors (TGFBR1 and TGFBR2) were described to cause LDS, hereby leading to impaired TGF-β signaling. More recently, TGF-β ligands, TGFB2 and TGFB3, as well as intracellular downstream effectors of the TGF-β pathway, SMAD2 and SMAD3, were shown to be involved in LDS.
